title: Complex PTSD
subtitle: PTSD plus persistent disturbances in self-organisation
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating complex ptsd across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain complex ptsd in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in complex ptsd.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to complex ptsd.

sections.explainSimply: Complex PTSD includes core PTSD symptoms alongside affect dysregulation, negative self-concept and relational disturbance.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Its neuroscience overlaps with PTSD, depression and dissociation; there is no validated biomarker that distinguishes it clinically.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: ICD-11 supports the diagnosis, while DSM frameworks organise these features differently. Assessment remains phenomenological and contextual.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of complex ptsd as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need complex ptsd to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not claim scans can separate PTSD from complex PTSD.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use complex ptsd to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses complex ptsd to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not claim scans can separate PTSD from complex PTSD. Evidence classification: established diagnostic construct; biomarkers insufficient.
